questions.question: Cortes reached the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan in 1519 with a few hundred men. What did the Spanish find there?
options: A city larger than any in Spain, built on a lake
A network of caves the Aztec nobility lived inside
A fortified hilltop town of a few thousand people
A ruined settlement recently abandoned by its people
questions.answer: A city larger than any in Spain, built on a lake
questions.explanation: Tenochtitlan held perhaps 200,000 people, several times the population of contemporary Seville or London, built on an island in Lake Texcoco with causeways, aqueducts and floating gardens. The Spanish accounts describe soldiers doubting what they were seeing. Within two years it was destroyed, mostly by smallpox, which killed a large share of the population before the final siege, and by tens of thousands of Indigenous allies who resented Aztec tribute demands. Mexico City sits on top of it.
questions.memory_hook: Tenochtitlan had maybe 200,000 people, bigger than Seville or London, on an island with causeways, aqueducts and floating gardens. Spanish soldiers wrote that they doubted their own eyes. Smallpox and tens of thousands of resentful Indigenous allies destroyed it inside two years. Mexico City is built on the rubble.

questions.question: The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on which date?
options: January 1, 1863
July 4, 1862
April 9, 1865
September 22, 1862
questions.explanation: President Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation took effect on January 1, 1863, declaring that enslaved people in Confederate states in rebellion were free. It was issued after the Union victory at Antietam in September 1862 gave Lincoln the political standing to make such a declaration. The 13th Amendment, which permanently abolished slavery throughout the US, was ratified in December 1865.
questions.memory_hook: Emancipation Proclamation = January 1, 1863. New Year's Day. Lincoln waited for a Union victory before issuing it — he didn't want it to look like desperation. It didn't immediately free anyone but changed the moral character of the Civil War forever.

questions.question: Constantinople fell to Ottoman forces in 1453 after surviving sieges for a thousand years. What broke the walls?
options: Enormous cannon cast specifically for the siege
An earthquake that collapsed a section of wall
A tunnel dug beneath the harbour defences
Betrayal by Venetian mercenaries inside the city
questions.answer: Enormous cannon cast specifically for the siege
questions.explanation: The Theodosian Walls had held off attackers since the fifth century. Mehmed II commissioned a Hungarian engineer named Orban to cast bombards, one reportedly over eight metres long, firing stone balls of half a tonne. They were slow, needing hours between shots, but the walls could not be repaired fast enough. Constantine XI died in the fighting. The fall is often used to mark the end of the Middle Ages, and gunpowder ending the age of the high stone wall.
questions.memory_hook: The Theodosian Walls had held for a thousand years. Mehmed II hired a Hungarian engineer, Orban, to cast bombards over eight metres long firing half-tonne stone balls. They took hours to reload but the walls could not be patched fast enough. It is often used to mark the end of the Middle Ages.

questions.question: In American football, what is a 'Hail Mary' play?
options: A defensive blitz sending every linebacker
A field goal attempted from beyond midfield
A kickoff returned the length of the field
A long, desperate forward pass into the end zone
questions.answer: A long, desperate forward pass into the end zone
questions.explanation: A Hail Mary is a long forward pass thrown in desperation near the end of a game with little time remaining, typically when the trailing team needs a touchdown. The term is associated with a prayer — you throw the ball and 'pray' it's caught. The name was popularized by Roger Staubach of the Dallas Cowboys after a 1975 playoff win. Such passes rarely work, but when they do, they produce some of football's most memorable moments.
questions.memory_hook: Hail Mary = desperate long pass. Named after a prayer. Roger Staubach coined the term in 1975 after throwing one. It almost never works, which is why it's desperate. But when it does — Doug Flutie, 1984, one of football's most iconic plays.

questions.question: Tiger Woods won the 1997 Masters by twelve strokes at twenty-one. What did Augusta National do afterward?
options: Lengthened the course, a change nicknamed Tiger-proofing
Banned players under twenty-five from entering
Introduced a handicap system for younger competitors
Changed the green jacket ceremony to exclude the press
questions.answer: Lengthened the course, a change nicknamed Tiger-proofing
questions.explanation: Woods finished at 18 under, the lowest score in tournament history, winning by the largest margin ever. Augusta responded over following years by adding length and rough, changes the press dubbed Tiger-proofing, and other courses followed. He was also the first Black or Asian winner at a club that had not admitted a Black member until 1990 and had required players to use its own caddies, all Black, until 1983.
questions.memory_hook: Woods finished 18 under and won by twelve, both records. Augusta responded by adding length and rough, which the press called Tiger-proofing, and other courses copied it. He was also the first Black winner at a club that admitted no Black members until 1990.

questions.question: Jordan Peele's Get Out (2017) was made for about $4.5 million. What did it achieve at the Oscars?
options: Peele won Best Director on his first ever feature film
It won Best Picture, the lowest-budget film ever to do so
It became the first horror film ever nominated for Best Picture
Peele became the first Black winner of Best Original Screenplay
questions.answer: Peele became the first Black winner of Best Original Screenplay
questions.explanation: Get Out grossed over $250 million against a $4.5 million budget and earned four nominations including Picture and Director. Peele won Original Screenplay, the first Black writer to do so. Horror is chronically overlooked by the Academy, though The Exorcist and The Silence of the Lambs had been nominated for Best Picture before, and Silence won. Peele had been known almost entirely for sketch comedy beforehand.
questions.memory_hook: Made for $4.5 million, grossed over $250 million, four Oscar nominations. Peele won Original Screenplay, the first Black writer to take it. Horror rarely gets Academy attention, though Silence of the Lambs had won Best Picture in 1992. Peele was a sketch comedian before this.

questions.question: Deadwood (HBO, 2004-2006), set in an 1870s mining camp, is praised for its language. What was David Milch's approach?
options: Modern profanity for period effect, Shakespearean structure
No script at all; dialogue was delivered orally each morning
Every episode drawn directly from real Deadwood court records
Dialogue written throughout in Shakespearean iambic pentameter
questions.answer: Modern profanity for period effect, Shakespearean structure
questions.explanation: David Milch (NYPD Blue) made a conscious decision to use modern profanity rather than 19th-century insults because the emotional impact would be lost. The show's elaborate, often digressive monologues — particularly from Ian McShane's Al Swearengen — recall Shakespearean soliloquy. Milch structured the camp itself as an emerging society inventing its own law and morality without outside governance — a frontier political experiment. HBO cancelled it after Season 3, leaving storylines unresolved; a 2019 film reunion concluded the story. McShane's Swearengen is considered one of TV's great anti-heroes.
questions.memory_hook: Deadwood uses modern profanity by design — period-accurate 19th-century obscenity would be meaningless to viewers, Milch argued. The camp's Shakespearean monologues and improvised frontier law-making are the real subject; Ian McShane's Swearengen is one of TV's great villains.

questions.question: Pearl Jam's Ten and Nirvana's Nevermind both came out in 1991. What set the two bands against each other?
options: Their labels forced them to tour together for a year
They were suing each other over a shared band name
Both had claimed the same producer exclusively
Cobain called Pearl Jam corporate sell-outs in the press
questions.answer: Cobain called Pearl Jam corporate sell-outs in the press
questions.explanation: Cobain publicly attacked Pearl Jam as careerists riding a movement they had not built, singling out Eddie Vedder. Vedder mostly declined to respond, and the two reconciled somewhat, slow-dancing together at the 1992 MTV awards. Ten actually outsold Nevermind over time. Pearl Jam then spent years fighting Ticketmaster over service fees, testifying before Congress in 1994, which cost them the ability to tour normally.
questions.memory_hook: Cobain called Pearl Jam corporate careerists in the press and named Eddie Vedder. Vedder largely stayed quiet, and they ended up slow-dancing together at the 1992 MTV awards. Ten outsold Nevermind eventually. Pearl Jam then took on Ticketmaster in Congress and lost the ability to tour normally.

questions.question: The Yangtze is Asia's longest river. What did China build across it that broke records?
options: The longest undersea rail tunnel anywhere in the world
A canal linking it directly to the Mekong delta in Vietnam
The first road bridge ever built from woven carbon fibre
The Three Gorges Dam, the largest power station on Earth
questions.answer: The Three Gorges Dam, the largest power station on Earth
questions.explanation: Three Gorges generates around 22,500 megawatts, more than any other power station of any kind. Building it displaced roughly 1.4 million people and submerged over 1,300 archaeological sites. The reservoir holds enough water that it measurably slowed Earth's rotation, lengthening the day by a few hundred-billionths of a second by shifting mass away from the axis. Sediment trapping and downstream ecological effects remain contested.
questions.memory_hook: Three Gorges makes about 22,500 megawatts, the biggest power station of any kind anywhere. It displaced 1.4 million people and drowned 1,300 archaeological sites. The reservoir holds so much water it measurably slowed Earth's rotation by shifting mass away from the axis.

questions.question: Most life on Earth runs on energy that traces back to sunlight. Which organisms break that rule entirely?
options: Deep-sea vent bacteria, which live on chemical energy
Arctic lichens, which run on geothermal heat alone
Deep-ocean fish, which generate their own light
Cave fungi, which draw energy directly from rock
questions.answer: Deep-sea vent bacteria, which live on chemical energy
questions.explanation: At hydrothermal vents thousands of metres down, bacteria oxidise hydrogen sulphide from the vent fluid to build sugars, a process called chemosynthesis. Entire ecosystems of tube worms, crabs and clams depend on them with no sunlight involved at any step. The discovery in 1977 at the Galapagos Rift overturned the assumption that all food chains begin with photosynthesis, and it reshaped where scientists look for life on moons like Europa and Enceladus.
questions.memory_hook: At hydrothermal vents, bacteria build sugars from hydrogen sulphide instead of sunlight, and whole ecosystems of tube worms and crabs run on them. Found in 1977 at the Galapagos Rift, it broke the rule that food chains start with photosynthesis, and it changed where we look for life on Europa.

questions.question: The Po Valley is Italy's agricultural and industrial heartland. What environmental problem does its geography create?
options: Annual flooding leaves half the valley unusable each spring
Volcanic ash carried from Etna regularly buries the farmland
Mountains on three sides trap Europe's worst air pollution
Saltwater intrusion has rendered much of the soil infertile
questions.answer: Mountains on three sides trap Europe's worst air pollution
questions.explanation: The Alps to the north and west and the Apennines to the south enclose the basin, and winter temperature inversions cap it, so emissions from dense industry, farming and traffic accumulate rather than dispersing. Particulate levels in Milan and Turin regularly rank among the worst in Europe. The same enclosure gives the valley its fertility and its fog. The Po itself has also been running dangerously low in recent drought years, threatening irrigation.
questions.memory_hook: The Alps and Apennines box the valley in on three sides, and winter inversions seal the lid, so industrial and farm emissions just sit there. Milan and Turin have some of Europe's worst particulate readings. The same enclosure is what makes the soil rich and the valley foggy.

questions.question: What is apoptosis — and why is it essential for normal development and disease prevention?
options: Programmed cell death, removing damaged or unneeded cells
Cellular energy production carried out in the mitochondria
Uncontrolled division of cells that have become cancerous
Replication of DNA in preparation for a cell to divide
questions.answer: Programmed cell death, removing damaged or unneeded cells
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is a highly regulated process of programmed cell death — cells essentially commit suicide in an orderly way, without triggering inflammation. It is essential for: embryonic development (fingers form when cells between them die), immune regulation (eliminating autoreactive T cells), and cancer prevention (eliminating mutated cells before they proliferate). When apoptosis fails — cells that should die instead survive and divide — cancer can result. Many cancer treatments work by triggering apoptosis in tumor cells.
questions.memory_hook: Apoptosis = programmed cell death. Cells commit suicide on cue — orderly, without inflammation. Your fingers formed when cells between them died in the womb. Immune cells that attack 'self' are eliminated this way. When apoptosis fails, cells that should die keep dividing — that's cancer. Many cancer drugs work by restarting this process.
